correction.text: southern Ontario, the north shore of Lakes Ontario and Erie: the Upper Canada of 1791, west of the Ottawa River

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe. 'Upper Canada existed from its establishment on 26 December 1791 to 10 February 1841'; the 1791 act 'did not yet specify official borders'; the Province of Quebec page says the colony was divided 'at the Ottawa River'. Infobox area 258,999 km2 (1836); the gazetteer's Upper Canada region is 453,703 km2 (ratio 1.75, within the factor of two; it reaches lat 50 N, and the settled colony was southern Ontario). Soft until the Jay Treaty (1795).

Detroit was lost after Put-in-Bay (10 September 1813); the British captured Fort Niagara on 18 December 1813 and Lewiston on the 19th; Buffalo was burned on 30 December. region.text: southern Ontario, the north shore of Lakes Ontario and Erie: the Upper Canada of 1791, west of the Ottawa River

ledger.note: 1791: Upper Canada is created. 'Upper Canada became a political entity on 26 December 1791' by the Constitutional Act, split from the Province of Quebec (Province of Quebec page: 'divided the colony in two at the Ottawa River'). The Upper Canada page says the act 'did not yet specify official borders', so the region is the researcher's reading.
1796: the capital moves to York. 'On 1 February 1796, the capital of Upper Canada was moved from Newark (now Niagara-on-the-Lake) to York (now Toronto).'

ledger.note: 1812: the British capture Mackinac. The garrison 'immediately besieged and captured Mackinac' after Brock's order; the page gives no day.

ledger.note: 1812: war with the United States. 'The United States declared war on Britain on 18 June 1812'; the British 'immediately besieged and captured Mackinac' and Detroit surrendered on 16 August.

region.text: Detroit, surrendered by Hull on 16 August 1812

ledger.note: 1812: Detroit surrenders. 'He agreed to surrender on 16 August' (William Hull). The Upper Canada page has 'Detroit was captured by the British on 6 August 1812'.

region.text: the Niagara peninsula around Fort George and Newark, occupied by American forces from 27 May to 10 December 1813

ledger.note: 1813: the Americans take the Niagara peninsula. Fort George fell on 27 May 1813 'without serious losses'; York, the capital, had been attacked on 27 April 1813.

region.text: Detroit, surrendered by Hull on 16 August 1812

ledger.note: 1813: Detroit is lost. The American victory at Put-in-Bay on 10 September 1813 'forced the British to withdraw from Detroit'; the Battle of the Thames followed on 5 October.

region.text: the Niagara peninsula around Fort George and Newark, occupied by American forces from 27 May to 10 December 1813

ledger.note: 1813: the Americans leave the Niagara peninsula. 'They set fire to the village of Newark' on 10 December 1813 as they abandoned the area.

region.text: Fort Niagara and Lewiston on the American bank of the Niagara River, taken in December 1813

ledger.note: 1813: Fort Niagara. 'The British captured it on 18 December' (the page; others give the 19th), then stormed neighbouring Lewiston on the 19th and burned Buffalo on 30 December.

wars.outcome: Britain held Mackinac and Detroit from 1812 (Detroit to September 1813), the Americans occupied the Niagara peninsula May-December 1813 and the British took Fort Niagara in December 1813; 'The Treaty of Ghent restored the pre-war territorial status quo' (ratified 17 February 1815).
wars.note: Upper Canada page: 'In 1812, war broke out between Great Britain and the United States, leading to several battles in Upper Canada.' The belligerent 'kingdom-of-great-britain' is the metropole's slug.

wars.name: Upper Canada Rebellion
wars.outcome: An insurrection 'against the oligarchic government of the Family Compact in December 1837'; 'resistance lingered until 1838 (and became more violent)'; no territory changed hands.

certainty.note: The 1791 act 'did not yet specify official borders'; the boundary with the United States was unsettled.

'The 1795 Jay Treaty officially set the borders between British North America and the United States' (Upper Canada page): the southern border through the lakes is sharp; the northern and western limits of the colony stay soft.

notes: Not a Cliopatria row (Cliopatria draws these years inside 'British Colonial Empire'). Pages: Upper Canada, War of 1812, Province of Quebec (1763-1791) for the 1791 split (three). Not on the pages: the Ottawa River as the boundary (the Upper Canada page does not give it; the Quebec page does), the Treaty of Ghent signing day (24 December 1814, not on the page), the American occupation of York beyond the 27 April 1813 attack, the Rush-Bagot Agreement, the Jay Treaty's evacuation of the western posts in 1796. Disagreements: Detroit captured 6 August 1812 (Upper Canada page) vs surrendered 16 August (War of 1812 page); Fort Niagara 18 December (War of 1812 page). The capital at Kingston in 1841 belongs to the Province of Canada. The two gazetteer-region caveats: the 'Upper Canada' region reaches lat 50 N, larger than the colony of 1836 (258,999 km2).
